metric_rationale: Calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the Take The Best (TTB) prediction. The experimental design specifically pits the highest-validity cue (favored by TTB) against the sum of the remaining lower-validity cues (favored by WADD). Because TTB is a non-compensatory, one-reason heuristic, it will consistently choose the option with the highest validity discriminating cue. By contrast, WADD integrates all cues, and since the sum of the remaining cues outweighs the top cue in these trials, WADD will systematically choose the opposite option. Thus, this metric will be close to 1 for TTB and close to 0 for WADD, providing maximum discrimination.

In the chosen experimental design, all 6 trial types are structurally compensatory: the single most valid discriminating cue always points to Option A, while the sum of the remaining less-valid discriminating cues always points to Option B. Consequently, Take The Best (TTB) will invariably choose Option A (response = 0) because it stops at the first discriminating cue. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model integrates all cues, and since the sum of the validities of the lower cues outweighs the top cue, WADD will systematically choose Option B (response = 1). Therefore, the overall proportion of choices for Option B (the mean of the 'response' column) will be close to 0 for TTB and close to 1 for WADD.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses the option favored by the single highest-validity cue (f0) on 'conflict' trials. These are trials where the TTB-favored option has very few positive cues overall (sum <= 2), while the opposing option has many positive lower-validity cues (sum >= 4). A pure WADD model will strongly tend to choose the option with more positive cues, resulting in a low score on this metric. In contrast, the Strategy Mixture model, which periodically relies on the non-compensatory TTB heuristic, will choose the f0-favored option much more frequently, leading to a significantly higher score.

This metric calculates the difference in choice probability for the WADD-favored option between 'strong agreement' trials (where both WADD and TTB favor the same option) and 'strong conflict' trials (where WADD strongly favors one option, but TTB favors the other). Under the pure WADD theory, choice probabilities are driven by the large WADD score difference in both trial types, so the metric (difference in probabilities) will be close to 0. Under the Mixture theory, the choice probability on conflict trials is artificially capped by the mixture weight (wadd_prob) because the TTB component consistently votes against the WADD-favored option, resulting in a large positive metric.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option favored by the most valid cue (cue 1, validity 0.95). In the Advocated theory, the mixture of Take-The-Best (which strictly follows cue 1) and Weighted Additive (which heavily weights cue 1) will produce a high alignment rate. In contrast, the Competing theory relies on Equal Weights (Tallying) combined with a very high guessing rate (lapse >= 0.8). Since Tallying often ties or even opposes cue 1 in this specific experimental design, and the high lapse rate dilutes any systematic preference, the Competing theory will predict an alignment rate very close to or slightly below 0.5. This creates a strong and consistent divergence between the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of times subjects choose Option A in Trial 1, where Option A has fewer positive cues (2) but they are the most valid, while Option B has more positive cues (3) but they are less valid. The Advocated theory (Equal Weights + High Lapse) predicts subjects will slightly favor Option B (since 3 > 2) or be completely indifferent due to high lapsing, resulting in a metric value <= 0.5. The Competing theory (TTB + WADD) predicts a strong preference for Option A, because both Take-The-Best (relying on the 0.95 cue) and Weighted Additive (1.85 vs 1.60) strongly favor A, resulting in a metric value > 0.5. This clear opposition in choice direction will yield a highly significant discrimination.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option containing the single highest-validity cue (cue 0). The Advocated theory (Single-Cue Focus) predicts that subjects will systematically favor the option with the highest-validity cue whenever they do not lapse, yielding a concordance greater than 0.5. Conversely, the Competing theory (Equal Weights) tallies the total number of cues. The experimental design intentionally pits the highest-validity cue against the sheer quantity of cues, such that the Equal Weights model consistently predicts choices contrary to the single best cue, yielding a concordance below 0.5.

This metric isolates 'conflict' trials where the Equal Weights (Tallying) heuristic and the Single-Cue (Best Cue) heuristic point in opposite directions. It calculates the proportion of choices on these trials that align with the Tallying prediction. The Advocated theory (Tallying) will score above 0.5, whereas the Competing theory (Single-Cue Focus) will score below 0.5, maximizing the discriminability between the two theories.
